figures.sourceCaption: Figure 1: AegisVox separates voice identity from identifying words. SeedVC converts every turn using one consistent surrogate voice per source speaker. The lexical renderer changes only converted turns with planned identifier replacements; the remaining converted turns pass directly to reconstruction. F5-TTS is the illustrated renderer, and VoiceCraft is the matched alternative. PHI denotes protected health information.

Figure 2: Clinical controls and matched renderer effects on 25,778 source CAPs from 390 conversations. (a) Fresh original-audio ASR supplies the reference, not clinical ground truth. (b) F5-TTS minus VoiceCraft effects in percentage points (pp), with 95% conversation-cluster intervals. Similar strict preservation coexists with more model-labeled contradictions.

Figure 3: Final-waveform linkage under evaluation-label-selected score direction. F5-TTS minus VoiceCraft effects use all-turn samples (809 profiles, 390 conversations) or planned-edit regions (291 profiles, 204 conversations). Bars are 95% clustered CIs. Lower EER means easier source linkage.

figures.sourceCaption: Figure 2: Bidirectional modality misrouting under audio-visual interference. CaRe mitigates these errors by steering the fused representation toward the selected modality-specific branch.
Figure 3: Target-branch recovery among incorrect joint predictions on CMM and AVHBench (%).

Figure 1: Overview of CaRe. Given audio-visual inputs and a question, CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to select a candidate modality, detects decision conflicts between the joint and counterfactual branches, and applies confidence-adaptive residual intervention at selected decoder layers with strengths decayed across depth.

Figure 8: Sensitivity to the intervention strength scale \lambda_{\alpha} on CMM. Lines report accuracy, while bars show the numbers of helpful and harmful prediction changes. Stars denote the default setting \lambda_{\alpha}=1.

figures.sourceCaption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed HE-NAC system.
Fig. 3: Mean MUSHRA scores for each condition with 95% confidence intervals for the mean. Nominal bitrates (kbps) are indicated under the coded systems.

Fig. 2: Overall reconstruction flow of the proposed three-stage training paradigm. Gray segments denote components used only during training: they provide blind-upsampled, bitrate-free priors to the next stage, but are omitted (filtered out) at inference.

Fig. 4: Rate–distortion (STFT error) curves shown per frequency band (0-3, 3-6, 6-16 kHz, and full-band) over the 13-23 kbps range. DAC (baseline) scales its bitrate by controlling the number of codebooks, ranging from 18 to 31, defined by its single bottleneck. HE-NAC (proposed) keeps 16 codebooks in its CB, but then gradually increases the MB codebooks from 1 to 4, as well as the HB codebooks from 0 to 2. Each DAC datapoint is annotated with its total number of codebooks, J, whereas each HE-NAC datapoint is annotated with the complete branch-specific allocation (J_{\mathrm{CB}},J_{\mathrm{MB}},J_{\mathrm{HB}}). The third entry, J_{\mathrm{HB}}, therefore denotes the number of codebooks allocated to the HB branch. When J_{\mathrm{HB}}=0, no dedicated HB residual is transmitted and the 6-16 kHz band is reconstructed solely through blind upsampling from the CB and MB stages. Increasing J_{\mathrm{HB}} to 1 and 2 progressively enables dedicated HB residual coding, explaining the sharp reduction in HB distortion.
